claim: Nonribosomal peptides represent a large class of metabolites with pharmaceutical relevance.
source: Nonribosomal peptides represent a large class of metabolites with pharmaceutical relevance.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about nonribosomal peptides.

claim: Pteridines, such as pterins, folates, and flavins, are heterocyclic metabolites that often serve as redox-active cofactors.
source: Pteridines, such as pterins, folates, and flavins, are heterocyclic metabolites that often serve as redox-active cofactors.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about pteridines.

claim: An unprecedented nonribosomal peptide synthetase-like-pteridine synthase hybrid biosynthetic gene cluster was discovered in Photorhabdus luminescens using genome synteny analysis.
source: Here, we discovered an unprecedented nonribosomal peptide synthetase-like-pteridine synthase hybrid biosynthetic gene cluster in Photorhabdus luminescens using genome synteny analysis.
evidence: The authors report their discovery using genome synteny analysis.

claim: P. luminescens is a Gammaproteobacterium that undergoes phenotypic variation and can have both pathogenic and mutualistic roles.
source: P. luminescens is a Gammaproteobacterium that undergoes phenotypic variation and can have both pathogenic and mutualistic roles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about P. luminescens, likely supported by citations in the full text.

claim: The genetic locus affects the regulation of quorum sensing and secondary metabolic enzymes.
source: Through extensive gene deletion, pathway-targeted molecular networking, quantitative proteomic analysis, and NMR, we show that the genetic locus affects the regulation of quorum sensing and secondary metabolic enzymes and encodes new pteridine metabolites functionalized with cis-amide acyl-side chains, termed pepteridine A (1) and B (2).
evidence: The authors used quantitative proteomic analysis to demonstrate this effect.

claim: The genetic locus encodes new pteridine metabolites functionalized with cis-amide acyl-side chains, termed pepteridine A (1) and B (2).
source: Through extensive gene deletion, pathway-targeted molecular networking, quantitative proteomic analysis, and NMR, we show that the genetic locus affects the regulation of quorum sensing and secondary metabolic enzymes and encodes new pteridine metabolites functionalized with cis-amide acyl-side chains, termed pepteridine A (1) and B (2).
evidence: The authors used NMR and other techniques to characterize these new metabolites.

claim: The pepteridines are produced in the pathogenic phenotypic variant.
source: The pepteridines are produced in the pathogenic phenotypic variant and represent the first reported metabolites to be synthesized by a hybrid NRPS-pteridine pathway.
evidence: The authors demonstrated this through analysis of genetically locked variants.

claim: The pepteridines represent the first reported metabolites to be synthesized by a hybrid NRPS-pteridine pathway.
source: The pepteridines are produced in the pathogenic phenotypic variant and represent the first reported metabolites to be synthesized by a hybrid NRPS-pteridine pathway.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the discovery based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Nonribosomal peptides are constructed from a highly diverse pool of potential proteinogenic and nonproteinogenic amino acid building blocks.
source: Nonribosomal peptides are a structurally and functionally privileged class of natural products constructed from a highly diverse pool of potential proteinogenic and nonproteinogenic amino acid building blocks (Walsh et al., 2013; Walsh, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Walsh et al., 2013 and Walsh, 2016.

claim: Vancomycin, daptomycin, penicillin, and cyclosprin are well-known pharmacologically relevant nonribosomal peptides.
source: Members of the family include well-known pharmacologically relevant agents, such as vancomycin, daptomycin, penicillin, cyclosprin, and many others.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nonribosomal peptides.

claim: The core catalytic domains of a minimal nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) extender module include condensation (C), adenylation (A), and peptidyl-carrier protein (PCP) domains.
source: The core catalytic domains of a minimal nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) extender module include condensation (C), adenylation (A), and peptidyl-carrier protein (PCP, a.k.a., thiolation, T) domains.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NRPS structure.

claim: The NRPS first selects its cognate amino acid from the available substrate pool, a step controlled by the selectivity of the A domain.
source: The NRPS first selects its cognate amino acid from the available substrate pool, a step controlled by the selectivity of the A domain, activates it as an aminoacyl adenylate, and subsequently loads it onto the PCP domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NRPS mechanism.

claim: The C domain typically catalyzes the formation of a trans-amide bond establishing individual peptide backbone linkages through nucleophilic attack of the free amino group present on a downstream aminoacyl-PCP on the upstream peptidyl-PCP.
source: The C domain then typically catalyzes the formation of a trans-amide bond establishing individual peptide backbone linkages through nucleophilic attack of the free amino group present on a downstream aminoacyl-PCP on the upstream peptidyl-PCP.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NRPS mechanism.

claim: NRPS-polyketide synthase (PKS) hybrid pathways produce important molecules, including rapamycin, bleomycin, epothilone, and colibactin.
source: Of note are the NRPS-polyketide synthase (PKS) hybrid pathways, which produce important molecules, including rapamycin, bleomycin, epothilone, colibactin, and others.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hybrid NRPS-PKS pathways.

claim: Pteridines, such as the cofactors biopterin and folate, are derived from guanosine triphosphate (GTP).
source: In contrast to the 'assembly line' logic of the majority of NRPSs, pteridines, such as the cofactors biopterin and folate, are derived from guanosine triphosphate (GTP) (Brown, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brown, 2006.

claim: Pteridines are composed of fused pyrimidine and pyrazine rings.
source: Pteridines are composed of fused pyrimidine and pyrazine rings, and natural pteridines are typically functionalized at the C-6 position of the pteridine core (vide infra).
evidence: This is established knowledge about pteridine structure.

claim: Natural pteridines are typically functionalized at the C-6 position of the pteridine core.
source: Pteridines are composed of fused pyrimidine and pyrazine rings, and natural pteridines are typically functionalized at the C-6 position of the pteridine core (vide infra).
evidence: This is established knowledge about pteridine chemistry.

claim: The electronic properties of the pteridine scaffold underlie its role in redox active cofactors critical to a host of metabolic transformations, such as hydroxylation of aromatic compounds and generation of the neurotransmitter nitric oxide.
source: The electronic properties of this scaffold underlie its role in redox active cofactors critical to a host of metabolic transformations, such as hydroxylation of aromatic compounds and generation of the neurotransmitter nitric oxide (Groehn et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Groehn et al., 2000.

claim: Functionalized pteridines serve as reactants in a number of one-carbon group transfer reactions in metabolism.
source: Additionally, functionalized pteridines serve as reactants in a number of one-carbon group transfer reactions in metabolism and, more recently, were implicated in catalysis of 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition-mediated decarboxylation reactions (Payne et al., 2015; White et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about pteridine function.

claim: Functionalized pteridines were recently implicated in catalysis of 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition-mediated decarboxylation reactions.
source: Additionally, functionalized pteridines serve as reactants in a number of one-carbon group transfer reactions in metabolism and, more recently, were implicated in catalysis of 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition-mediated decarboxylation reactions (Payne et al., 2015; White et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Payne et al., 2015 and White et al., 2015.

claim: The increase in genomic sequence information from diverse microbial sources has highlighted enormous untapped metabolic potential for discovery of novel nonribosomal peptides and pteridines.
source: The increase in genomic sequence information from diverse microbial sources has highlighted enormous untapped metabolic potential for discovery of novel nonribosomal peptides and pteridines among other metabolite groups, including groups synthesized by new enzyme classes (Cimermancic et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cimermancic et al., 2014.

claim: Bacterial secondary metabolic pathways encoding many metabolites often reside on genomic islands as a result of horizontal gene transfer events during evolution.
source: As a result of horizontal gene transfer events during evolution, it is known that the bacterial secondary metabolic pathways encoding many of these metabolites often reside on genomic islands (Shankar et al., 2006; Penn et al., 2009; Ziemert et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shankar et al., 2006; Penn et al., 2009; Ziemert et al., 2014.

claim: Genome synteny analyses platforms enable in silico visualization of co-localized genetic loci among phylogenetically related organisms.
source: Genome synteny analyses platforms enable in silico visualization of co-localized genetic loci among phylogenetically related organisms and represent general tools to aid in identifying genomic islands.
evidence: This is established knowledge about genome synteny analysis.

claim: The authors have previously used genome synteny analysis to aid in identification of 'atypical pathways' and to determine the biocatalytic functions of hypothetical proteins located on genomic islands.
source: We have previously used genome synteny analysis to aid in identification of 'atypical pathways' and to determine the biocatalytic functions of hypothetical proteins located on genomic islands (Guo and Crawford, 2014; Vizcaino et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: P. luminescens is a Gram-negative Gammaproteobacterium that undergoes stochastic phenotypic variation.
source: P. luminescens is a Gram-negative Gammaproteobacterium that undergoes stochastic phenotypic variation, and through the use of genetically 'locked' variants (Somvanshi et al., 2012), we show that the pepteridines are produced in a specific variant associated with pathogenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about P. luminescens, supported by citation to Somvanshi et al., 2012.

claim: Allelic-exchange mutagenesis in P. luminescens and comparative quantitative proteomic analysis demonstrated that when the LysR-type transcriptional repressor is derepressed (ΔhexA), the pepteridine genetic locus positively affects pyrone quorum sensing and select secondary metabolic pathways.
source: Allelic-exchange mutagenesis in P. luminescens and comparative quantitative proteomic analysis further reveal that the genetic locus affects production of several groups of proteins related to the biosynthesis of known quorum sensing and secondary metabolite systems.
evidence: This is based on the authors' proteomic data.

claim: P. luminescens is a Gammaproteobacterium mutualistically associated with nematodes, and the pair prey on insect larvae.
source: P. luminescens is a Gammaproteobacterium mutualistically associated with nematodes, and the pair prey on insect larvae (Waterfield et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Waterfield et al., 2009.

claim: P. luminescens produces an assortment of bioactive molecules and antibiotics to regulate its mutualistic and pathogenic interactions.
source: P. luminescens produces an assortment of bioactive molecules and antibiotics to regulate its mutualistic and pathogenic interactions (Vizcaino et al., 2014b; Challinor and Bode, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vizcaino et al., 2014b and Challinor and Bode, 2015.

claim: The Photorhabdus genus rivals the Streptomyces genus in terms of the number of secondary metabolic pathways in a given genome.
source: Consequently, this genus, which includes one human pathogen, rivals the Streptomyces genus in terms of the number of secondary metabolic pathways in a given genome (Duchaud et al., 2003; Tobias et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Duchaud et al., 2003 and Tobias et al., 2016.

claim: A genomic island (plu2792-plu2799) harboring mixed NRPS-pteridine synthase machinery was identified using the MicroScope bioinformatics platform.
source: Using the MicroScope bioinformatics platform, we identified a genomic island (plu2792-plu2799, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), harboring mixed NRPS-pteridine synthase machinery (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis and shown in figures.

claim: Protein sequence homology analysis demonstrated predicted pteridine biosynthetic enzymes, such as GTP cyclohydrolase (GTPCH) Ι, 6-pyruvoyltetrahydropterin synthase, pteridine reductase, and pteridine pyrophosphokinase in the genomic island.
source: Protein sequence homology analysis demonstrated predicted pteridine biosynthetic enzymes, such as GTP cyclohydrolase (GTPCH) Ι, 6-pyruvoyltetrahydropterin synthase, pteridine reductase, and pteridine pyrophosphokinase.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: A NRPS carrier protein (thiolation domain, T) and a condensation domain (C) were genetically fused to a pyruvate dehydrogenase E2-like subunit (plu2796).
source: Interestingly, a NRPS carrier protein (thiolation domain, T) and a condensation domain (C) were genetically fused to a pyruvate dehydrogenase E2-like subunit (plu2796).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of the gene sequence.

claim: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (E1, E2, and E3 subunits) is a well-studied set of enzymes that converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA.
source: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (E1, E2, and E3 subunits) is a well-studied set of enzymes that converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA (Patel and Roche, 1990), serving as a key metabolic bridge between glycolysis and the citric acid cycle.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Patel and Roche, 1990.

claim: A complementary E1-like subunit is also encoded in the pathway.
source: A complementary E1-like subunit is also encoded in the pathway.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of the gene cluster.

claim: This pathway was not detected by early versions of the antiSMASH algorithm used for identifying the biosynthetic pathways of secondary metabolites.
source: This pathway was not detected by early versions of the antiSMASH algorithm (Blin et al., 2013) used for identifying the biosynthetic pathways of secondary metabolites; however, recent integration of the ClusterFinder algorithm which aids in identifying divergent biosynthetic gene clusters of unknown classes (Cimermancic et al., 2014; Weber et al., 2015) allowed detection of part of the pathway (plu2796-plu2798) as a likely pathway of secondary metabolic enzymes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Blin et al., 2013; Cimermancic et al., 2014; Weber et al., 2015.

claim: Recent integration of the ClusterFinder algorithm allowed detection of part of the pathway (plu2796-plu2798) as a likely pathway of secondary metabolic enzymes.
source: This pathway was not detected by early versions of the antiSMASH algorithm (Blin et al., 2013) used for identifying the biosynthetic pathways of secondary metabolites; however, recent integration of the ClusterFinder algorithm which aids in identifying divergent biosynthetic gene clusters of unknown classes (Cimermancic et al., 2014; Weber et al., 2015) allowed detection of part of the pathway (plu2796-plu2798) as a likely pathway of secondary metabolic enzymes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cimermancic et al., 2014 and Weber et al., 2015.

claim: The hybrid NRPS-pteridine genomic island was cloned without its clustered regulatory protein (Plu2792) and placed under the control of a phage T7 promoter for heterologous expression in Escherichia coli BAP1.
source: We first cloned the hybrid NRPS-pteridine genomic island without its clustered regulatory protein (Plu2792) and placed it under the control of a phage T7 promoter for heterologous expression in Escherichia coli BAP1 (Pfeifer et al., 2001).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken by the authors, supported by citation to Pfeifer et al., 2001.

claim: Comparison of the culture broths from E. coli harboring the pathway relative to that of an empty vector control (pET28a) revealed a pathway-dependent yellow phenotype.
source: Comparison of the culture broths from E. coli harboring the pathway relative to that of an empty vector control (pET28a) revealed a pathway-dependent yellow phenotype (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on visual observation shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Initial comparative single quadrupole liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC/MS) analysis of butanol extracts revealed two dramatically increased peaks in the broth harboring the pathway.
source: Initial comparative single quadrupole liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC/MS) analysis of their butanol extracts revealed two dramatically increased peaks in the broth harboring the pathway (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on LC/MS data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The chemical structures of the small molecules attributed to these peaks were assigned as known 2-amino-4-oxopteridine small molecules, 7,8-dihydroxanthopterin (3) and pterin (4).
source: Through extensive 1D- and 2D-NMR, high-resolution-electrospray ionization-quadrupole-time-of-flight-mass spectrometry (HR-ESI-QTOF-MS), and LC/MS co-injections with authentic standards (Figure 2C–E and Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2), the chemical structures of the small molecules attributed to these peaks were assigned as known 2-amino-4-oxopteridine small molecules, 7,8-dihydroxanthopterin (3) and pterin (4).
evidence: This is based on NMR, MS, and co-injection data shown in figures.

claim: 224 molecular features in butanol extracts were dependent on the presence of the wild-type pathway relative to the control vector.
source: Relative to the control vector, we identified 224 molecular features in butanol extracts that were dependent on the presence of the wild-type pathway (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is based on comparative metabolomics data.

claim: 114 molecular features were dependent on the GTPCH Ι homolog, Plu2793.
source: Of these, 114 were dependent on the GTPCH Ι homolog, Plu2793, which is predicted to convert GTP to 7,8-dihydroneopterin triphosphate, initiating pteridine synthesis (Burg and Brown, 1968).
evidence: This is based on comparative metabolomics data and supported by citation to Burg and Brown, 1968.

claim: Plu2793 is predicted to convert GTP to 7,8-dihydroneopterin triphosphate, initiating pteridine synthesis.
source: Of these, 114 were dependent on the GTPCH Ι homolog, Plu2793, which is predicted to convert GTP to 7,8-dihydroneopterin triphosphate, initiating pteridine synthesis (Burg and Brown, 1968).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic prediction and supported by citation to Burg and Brown, 1968.

claim: 37 molecular features were dependent on the atypical dehydrogenase E2-NRPS fusion enzyme, Plu2796.
source: Thirty-seven molecular features were dependent on the atypical dehydrogenase E2-NRPS fusion enzyme, Plu2796, and only 12 were dependent on both.
evidence: This is based on comparative metabolomics data.

claim: 12 molecular features were dependent on both Plu2793 and Plu2796.
source: Thirty-seven molecular features were dependent on the atypical dehydrogenase E2-NRPS fusion enzyme, Plu2796, and only 12 were dependent on both.
evidence: This is based on comparative metabolomics data.

claim: Pathway-targeted molecular networking focuses on networking of metabolites dependent on the presence of a functional pathway.
source: Pathway-targeted molecular networking focuses on networking of metabolites dependent on the presence of a functional pathway (e.g., wild-type versus a secondary metabolic pathway mutant).
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used.

claim: Some deletions led to a decrease in, rather than complete abolishment of, select molecular feature production, indicating that substantial metabolic crosstalk occurs between this specific hybrid secondary metabolic pathway and primary metabolism.
source: Some deletions led to a decrease in, rather than complete abolishment of, select molecular feature production, indicating that substantial metabolic crosstalk occurs between this specific hybrid secondary metabolic pathway and primary metabolism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the metabolomics data.

claim: Two prominent metabolites were selected for NMR-based structural characterization through pathway-targeted molecular networking analysis.
source: Through this analysis, two prominent metabolites were selected for NMR-based structural characterization (Figure 3).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach shown in Figure 3.

claim: Pepteridine A (1) has the molecular formula C9H13N5O2 with [M+H]+ at m/z 224.1141.
source: Pepteridine A (1): white powder; UV (CH3OH) λmax (log ε) 282 (3.68), 222 (3.85) nm; 1H and 13C NMR spectra, see Table 2; HR-ESI-QTOF-MS [M+H]+m/z 224.1141 (calcd for C9H14N5O2, 224.1147).
evidence: This is based on HR-ESI-QTOF-MS data.

claim: Pepteridine B (2) has the molecular formula C8H11N5O2 with [M+H]+ at m/z 210.0985.
source: Pepteridine B (2): white powder; UV (CH3OH) λmax (log ε) 282 (3.48), 222 (3.75) nm; 1H and 13C NMR spectra, see Table 2; HR-ESI-QTOF-MS [M+H]+m/z 210.0985 (calcd for C8H12N5O2, 210.0991).
evidence: This is based on HR-ESI-QTOF-MS data.

claim: Compound 1 is characterized as 2-amino-5-propionyl-5,6,7,8-tetrahydropteridin-4(3H)-one.
source: These correlations established the connectivity of the propionyl group at N-5, thereby characterizing 1 as a 2-amino-5-propionyl-5,6,7,8-tetrahydropteridin-4(3H)-one (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on NMR data interpretation.

claim: Interpretation of NOESY NMR data and comparison of the proton chemical shifts at the pteridine C-6 to cis- and trans-amide analogs supported the cis-amide conformation of the acyl group at N-5 in solution.
source: Interpretation of NOESY NMR data and comparison of the proton chemical shifts at the pteridine C-6 to cis- and trans-amide analogs supported the cis-amide conformation of the acyl group at N-5 in solution (Figure 3—figure supplement 10) (Lanyon-Hogg et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on NOESY NMR data and supported by citation to Lanyon-Hogg et al., 2015.

claim: Compound 2 contains an acetyl group in place of the propionyl group in compound 1.
source: The critical difference between 1 and 2 was the absence of a CH2 signal in the NMR spectral data, supporting the assumption that 2 contains an acetyl group in place of the propionyl group in 1, and further HMBC NMR analysis and HR-ESI-QTOF-MS data confirmed this.
evidence: This is based on NMR and MS data.

claim: The biosynthetic route to the pepteridines consists of pteridine synthesis from GTP, acyl-synthesis via oxidative decarboxylation of α-keto acids, and NRPS-dependent condensation of these distinct substrates.
source: Combining the bioinformatic, genetic, and comparative metabolomic analyses with the new structures suggests a hybrid biosynthetic route to the pepteridines, consisting of pteridine synthesis from GTP, acyl-synthesis via oxidative decarboxylation of α-keto acids, and NRPS-dependent condensation of these distinct substrates (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a proposed biosynthetic mechanism based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The presence of predicted GTPCH Ι, 6-pyruvoyltetrahydropterin synthase, and pteridine reductase homologs in the pathway supports the formation and redox control of a tetrahydropterin substrate.
source: The presence of predicted GTPCH Ι, 6-pyruvoyltetrahydropterin synthase, and pteridine reductase homologs in the pathway supports the formation and redox control of a tetrahydropterin substrate.
evidence: This is an inference based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: The presence of the pyruvate-dehydrogenase-like E1 and E2-NRPS fusion enzymes supports derivation of the pepteridine acyl-appendages from α-keto acids through an analogous dehydrogenase mechanism.
source: The presence of the pyruvate-dehydrogenase-like E1 and E2-NRPS fusion enzymes supports derivation of the pepteridine acyl-appendages from α-keto acids through an analogous dehydrogenase mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: The pathway likely interacts with other pteridine and dehydrogenase biosynthetic enzymes encoded in the genome of the heterologous host, E. coli, such as the E3 subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.
source: It is likely, however, that the pathway interacts with other pteridine and dehydrogenase biosynthetic enzymes encoded in the genome of the heterologous host, E. coli, such as the E3 subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, which is required for lipoamide regeneration but absent from the pathway.
evidence: This is speculation based on the absence of the E3 subunit in the pathway.

claim: The CoA-derived carrier protein arm (T-domain) could be directly primed in place of CoA rather than producing an acyl-CoA.
source: Rather than producing an acyl-CoA, as in the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction, the CoA-derived carrier protein arm (T-domain) could be directly primed in place of CoA (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism shown in Figure 4.

claim: Analogous carrier protein priming mechanisms have been proposed for branched chain fatty acid substrate utilization in the formation of N-acyl-amides and the pristinamycin IIa streptogramin antibiotic.
source: Analogous carrier protein priming mechanisms have been proposed for branched chain fatty acid substrate utilization in the formation of N-acyl-amides and the pristinamycin IIa streptogramin antibiotic (Craig and Brady, 2011; Brachmann et al., 2012); and for a glycolicacyl-NRPS extender unit in formation of the naphthyridinomycin antitumor antibiotic (Peng et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Craig and Brady, 2011; Brachmann et al., 2012; Peng et al., 2012.

claim: The resulting loaded acyl-carrier protein in pepteridine biosynthesis would be unusually condensed with a free tetrahydropterin substrate by the atypical NRPS C domain to install the cis-amide acyl-linkage.
source: In contrast to these pathways, we propose that the resulting loaded acyl-carrier protein in pepteridine biosynthesis would be unusually condensed with a free tetrahydropterin substrate by the atypical NRPS C domain to install the cis-amide acyl-linkage.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism.

claim: It is currently unclear whether the C domain catalyzes direct cis-amide bond formation or whether a trans-amide is formed and then isomerized to the observed cis-conformation in the pepteridines.
source: It is currently unclear whether the C domain catalyzes direct cis-amide bond formation or whether a trans-amide is formed and then isomerized to the observed cis-conformation in the pepteridines.
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty in the mechanism.

claim: Pepteridine A (1) detection was completely abolished in the GTPCH Ι homolog mutant (Δplu2793), the 6-pyruvoyl-tetrahydropterin synthase homolog mutant (Δplu2794), and the atypical E2-NRPS mutant (Δplu2796).
source: Differential LC/HR-ESI-QTOF-MS analysis of butanol extracts demonstrated that pepteridine A (1) detection was completely abolished in the GTPCH Ι homolog mutant (Δplu2793), the 6-pyruvoyl-tetrahydropterin synthase homolog mutant (Δplu2794), and the atypical E2-NRPS mutant (Δplu2796), indicating a genetic requirement for both pteridine and NRPS biosynthetic machineries (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on LC/HR-ESI-QTOF-MS data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Production of pepteridine B (2) was substantially reduced in the Δplu2793 and Δplu2794 strains, and completely abolished in the Δplu2796 mutant strain.
source: Production of pepteridine B (2) was substantially reduced in the Δplu2793 and Δplu2794 strains, and completely abolished in the Δplu2796 mutant strain (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on LC/HR-ESI-QTOF-MS data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The minor residual production of compound 2 in the Δplu2793 and Δplu2794 strains is consistent with the observation that pterin (4) substrates can be detected at low abundance in the control strain (pET28a).
source: The minor residual production of 2 in these specific pteridine knockout strains is consistent with our observation that pterin (4) substrates can be detected at low abundance in the control strain (pET28a), further highlighting the metabolic crosstalk between this pathway and primary metabolism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data.

claim: A Plu2796 S434A point mutant was generated in the wild-type pathway construct to site-specifically inactivate the NRPS carrier protein domain.
source: To further demonstrate the biosynthetic dependence on the NRPS machinery, a Plu2796 S434A point mutant was generated in the wild-type pathway construct to site-specifically inactivate the NRPS carrier protein domain.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach.

claim: Assessment of pepteridine production from the Plu2796 S434A construct confirmed dependency on the NRPS machinery.
source: Assessment of pepteridine production from this construct in comparison with wild-type, Δplu2796, and control constructs confirmed dependency on the NRPS machinery (Figure 5B,D).
evidence: This is based on data shown in Figure 5B,D.

claim: Supplementation of bacterial cultures harboring the wild-type pathway with varying concentrations of free α-ketobutyrate and pyruvate resulted in enhanced production of the respective pepteridines in a dose-dependent manner.
source: We then supplemented bacterial cultures harboring the wild-type pathway with varying concentrations of free α-ketobutyrate and pyruvate and, as expected, observed enhanced production of the respective pepteridines in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on feeding experiments shown in figures.

claim: These studies link pepteridine production to α-ketoacid substrate availability rather than free acyl-CoA substrates.
source: Importantly, these studies link pepteridine production to α-ketoacid substrate availability (i.e., pyruvate and α-ketobutyrate) rather than free acyl-CoA substrates (i.e., acetyl- and propionyl-CoA).
evidence: This is an inference based on the feeding experiments.

claim: Photorhabdus bacteria are both pathogens to insects and mutualists to a specific nematode host.
source: Photorhabdus bacteria are both pathogens to insects and mutualists to a specific nematode host (Clarke, 2008; Waterfield et al., 2009; Clarke, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Clarke, 2008; Waterfield et al., 2009; Clarke, 2014.

claim: Photorhabdus asymbiotica can cause infections in humans.
source: Photorhabdus asymbiotica can also cause infections in humans (Gerrard et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gerrard et al., 2004.

claim: Photorhabdus bacteria undergo phenotypic variation, which is controlled by a stochastic invertible promoter switch.
source: To enhance their fitness for these variable host-bacteria objectives, Photorhabdus bacteria undergo phenotypic variation, which is controlled by a stochastic invertible promoter switch (Somvanshi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Somvanshi et al., 2012.

claim: The orientation of the promoter regulates the formation of P- and M-form phenotypic variants.
source: The orientation of the promoter regulates the formation of P- and M-form phenotypic variants.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Photorhabdus phenotypic variation.

claim: The P-form, typically the dominant variant in wild-type cultures, is pathogenic to insects.
source: The P-form, typically the dominant variant in wild-type cultures, is pathogenic to insects.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the P-form variant.

claim: The P-form switches to the M-form, a small colony variant, which adheres to specific cells in the nematode intestine.
source: The P-form switches to the M-form, a small colony variant, which adheres to specific cells in the nematode intestine.
evidence: This is established knowledge about phenotypic variation.

claim: The M-form phenotype is thought to participate in colonization of its mutualistic nematode host.
source: It is thought that the M-form phenotype participates in colonization of its mutualistic nematode host.
evidence: This is speculation based on established knowledge.

claim: Both pepteridines A and B could be detected in the pathogenic P-form phenotypic variant in M9-base medium.
source: In the M9-base medium, both pepteridines A and B could be detected in the pathogenic P-form phenotypic variant (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on LC/HR-ESI-QTOF-MS data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Under identical conditions, no pepteridine production was observed in the M-form.
source: However, under identical conditions, no production was observed in the M-form.
evidence: This is based on LC/HR-ESI-QTOF-MS data.

claim: These studies link pepteridine structure to phenotypic variant status and suggest that the pepteridines may participate in P-form biological activities.
